lead: An embedded system is a hardware platform plus a layered software stack. The hardware executes instructions and touches sensors and actuators; the software decides what to do. Where you draw the line between them is a design decision: a checksum can be a software loop or a hardware block. The usual stack is hardware, device drivers, middleware and application software. Each layer talks only to the layer below through a defined interface. This structure appears in a smart electricity meter, a washing machine and a car engine controller. It lets you change one layer without rewriting the rest.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for what an embedded system is, and Chapter 1.3 for the metrics the architecture must meet.

blocks.text: Hardware architecture is the set of physical blocks that execute instructions and touch the outside world. The processor core fetches and executes instructions. Program memory is usually flash: it keeps code when power is off. Data memory is SRAM: it holds variables and the stack while the program runs. A clock oscillator supplies the timing square wave; without it the core does not step. The reset circuit puts the processor into a known start state. The power supply converts the input to a regulated rail, and brown-out detection holds the processor in reset when the rail sags below a safe value. Peripherals are on-chip helpers: timers count time and generate waveforms, UART shifts bits for serial links, ADC converts an analogue sensor voltage to a number, and GPIO pins are general-purpose digital inputs and outputs. An internal bus carries addresses, data and control signals between the core, memories and peripherals. Outside the chip sit sensors, actuators and connectors. A classic microprocessor such as the 8086 brings out address, data and control buses as pins; a microcontroller keeps the same blocks inside one package.

items: Power-on reset: the supply has just risen.
External reset: a button is pressed.
Watchdog reset: software failed to service the watchdog.
Brown-out reset: the supply dipped below a safe level.

blocks.text: A pull-up resistor holds a line at logic high when nothing drives it. A pull-down holds it at logic low. A high-Z (floating) pin is not a logic level at all. Unused inputs get a pull-up or pull-down so they never float. Unit 3 and Unit 5 cover reset timing and watchdog use in detail.

Software architecture is a stack of layers. At the bottom is the hardware. The first software layer is the device drivers. They write and read hardware registers: set a GPIO pin high, load a timer count, read a UART data register. They hide register addresses from the rest of the code. Drivers are usually packaged with startup code and clock and memory initialisation as a board support package (BSP). Above the drivers is middleware: an RTOS or scheduler that decides which task runs next, protocol stacks such as a meter-reading protocol, a file system, and maths or graphics libraries. These are reusable services, not the product's own logic. At the top is application software, which holds the product's decisions: when to close a relay, how to compute a bill, what to show on the LCD. Communication software can sit side by side with application software above middleware: it moves bytes to a modem or a network, while the application decides what those bytes mean.

The rule is: a layer talks only to the layer below, through a defined interface. The application calls a middleware function; middleware calls a driver function; the driver writes a register. No layer reaches across. This lets you change the MCU and rewrite only the BSP.

sections.h3: Drawing the line and the tools

blocks.text: Where the hardware-software line falls is a design decision. A cyclic redundancy check (CRC) can be a software loop or a hardware block. Hardware is faster and uses less CPU time; software is cheaper to change and needs no extra silicon. Fixed, heavy, repeated work goes to hardware; changing policy stays in software. This partition is called hardware-software co-design; Unit 6 takes it further.

items: An IDE is the editor, project manager and debugger in one window.
A compiler translates C into the target instruction set; a cross-compiler runs on a PC but produces code for the MCU.
A simulator runs the program on the PC with a model of the MCU, so no board is needed.
An emulator or in-circuit debugger probes the real MCU and lets you stop at a breakpoint and read registers.
MCU internals — memory map, special function registers and interrupt vectors — are what the compiler and debugger must know.

figure.caption: The application sits at the top and the hardware at the bottom. Notice that each software layer calls only the layer below it.

examples.question: A smart electricity meter is built from an energy-measurement IC, a 32-bit MCU with 64 KB flash and 8 KB SRAM, a real-time clock, an LCD, an IR port, a UART to a modem, and a push button. The button connects the MCU input to 0 V when pressed; a 10 kΩ resistor pulls the same input to 3.3 V when the button is open. (a) List the hardware blocks and the external parts. (b) Assign the software layers. (c) Find the current through the pull-up and the power it wastes while the button is pressed.
steps: Hardware blocks: the energy-measurement IC feeds the MCU. Assume the MCU is a part with an on-chip RTC, UART and LCD driver; if the RTC is a separate chip it is an external part on the I²C bus. The MCU also contains the processor core, 64 KB flash and 8 KB SRAM. The LCD, IR port, modem, push button and 10 kΩ pull-up connect to the MCU. The clock oscillator, reset circuit and 3.3 V supply feed the MCU.
Software application layer: tariff and billing logic. It decides the price per unit and the bill.
Software middleware layer: the meter-reading protocol and RTC-based scheduling. These are reusable services above the drivers.
Software BSP layer: drivers for the measurement IC, UART, LCD and IR port. These read and write registers.
Button open: no current flows through the 10 kΩ resistor, so the input is held at 3.3 V, logic high. Button pressed: the input is 0 V and the resistor has 3.3 V across it.
examples.answer: The hardware is the measurement IC, MCU with flash/SRAM/RTC/UART/LCD driver, LCD, IR port, modem, oscillator, reset circuit and 3.3 V supply, plus the push button and 10 kΩ pull-up resistor; software is billing (application), meter protocol and RTC scheduling (middleware), and IC/UART/LCD/IR drivers (BSP); the pressed button draws 0.33 mA and the pull-up wastes 1.089 mW.

V=3.3
R=10000
I=V/R
P=V*I
print(round(I*1000,3))
print(round(P*1000,3))

traps: Calling the RTOS 'the application'. The RTOS is middleware; the application holds the billing, control or display logic.
Drawing a hardware block diagram with no clock, reset and power block. A processor without these three does not run.
Saying a pull-up sets a line to logic low. A pull-up sets logic high; a pull-down sets logic low.
Treating high-Z as a third logic level. It is no level, so unused inputs need a pull-up or pull-down.
Writing that application software writes registers directly. It calls middleware or a driver through a defined interface.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of the embedded stack from bottom to top.
quiz.a: Hardware, device drivers or board support package (BSP), middleware, application software.

quiz.q: What does a pull-up resistor do to a line?
quiz.a: It holds the line at logic high when nothing else drives it.

quiz.q: Why is brown-out detection needed in an embedded system?
quiz.a: When the supply voltage sags below a safe value, the processor may execute wrong instructions or corrupt memory. Brown-out detection holds the processor in reset until the supply is safe again.

quiz.q: State the layer interface rule and give one benefit.
quiz.a: A layer talks only to the layer below through a defined interface. Benefit: changing the MCU needs a rewrite of only the BSP, not the application.

quiz.q: A 4.7 kΩ pull-down holds an input at 0 V. A switch connects the input to 3.3 V when pressed. Find the current through the resistor while pressed.
A design moves a CRC calculation from software to a hardware block. Give one benefit and one cost.
quiz.a: Benefit: faster and less CPU time. Cost: less flexible, more silicon area, and a change needs a new chip revision.

quiz.q: Why can an unused CMOS input not be left floating?
quiz.a: A floating input is high-Z, so both transistors in the input stage may conduct. This wastes current and picks up noise. A pull-up or pull-down gives a definite logic level.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the hardware-software partition is argued with timing measurements and cost sheets, not only block diagrams. Automotive systems use standard layered software stacks so that application code can move between suppliers. Linux-based products put a bootloader, kernel and root file system under the same application layer idea. Search for hardware-software co-design, board support package and AUTOSAR layering to go further.
